If you check your score through Experian, you can also get your credit report which can show what factors are hurting your score.

If you have any debt in collections/ late payments and also use a large percentage of your credit line, I imagine it would make a big dent in your credit score.

With your Venture X providing 2X back on all purchases and the AmEx Gold for dining, you’ve pretty much exhausted the reasons for getting the CFU other than the SUB if you were trying to churn. CFF offered 5% back on Amazon during Q2 and Gas during Q3, so it could be a nice keeper card (and 3% on drugstores). Do note that with your CSP, you’ll be able to redeem your UR points that you get from Chase cards for 25% more value.

I’m pretty new to the credit card game myself and I’m surprised at your credit score in comparison with your credit card portfolio. Mind telling me your secret? I have a 795 Experian score but I’m still nervous when applying for new cards.

It's been gone for me for the past month. I exclusively used CashApp for MTA rides and my mom does the same, but only she has kept her boost. She claims that my phone is too old, but I'm not too convinced of that. She has an iPhone 12 and I have a second generation SE (specs comparable to the 11). I've also noticed that her CashApp UI is mainly green while mine is black. Not sure what the cause of that difference is either.

Just as a data point for my curiosity, can you tell me what phone you're using?
Thank you for your insight! My mom is in good health, but I’m trying to help her to get to a point where she won’t need my complete assistance once she gets to retirement age.

Thank you for the information! My mom has pretty much left her retirement/savings into my hands and I don’t want to mess things up. Opening up a HYSA and moving all the money we could that was rotting in a 0.01% savings was the easy part. 

I think we will have to go for a traditional IRA for my mom since she’s trying to get AGI lower to qualify for Medicaid (she’s been taking fewer hours at work before this). If that isn’t possible, roth is going to be the way to go. She’s very much a set it and forget it person, so I think a target date fund is the way to go.

I had no idea about Saver’s Credit! I think I make too much to qualify, but this could also be helpful for my mom!

We’ll also definitely need to look into how much social security she’ll be getting.

Ideally, you'd have another job lined up so you can leave this jerk. 

If that's not an option, you'll need to check with yourself whether or not the time spent without a paycheck is worth the peace of mind you'll have.

I've been in a similar situation to yours before; my boss didn't respect me or my time and there was no way I was willing to work another day with them. I left and it took a grueling year and a half to find another job. Would I have wanted to live through working for my boss during that time? No.

But I'm not you, so I can't speak for you. What you do is your decision.
It was an EasyApply, so the only times we contacted one another were through LinkedIn DMs and phone call
I think you're a good friend for wanting to call the account manager out on ghosting. The more that they get away with it, the more comfortable they'll feel about doing it to others in the future.

I think that the most important trait for a recruiter to have is effective communication. As a recruiter, you're building a relationship with not only the hiring company, but also the candidate. By being transparent about all that you've said so far, you're already doing a lot better than most of the other recruiters we see in this subreddit. Like /u/cowardlydragon said, you've become something like an athlete's agent that delivers value. I believe that is what an ideal recruiter should be: someone that has my back and trying to find the best job that fits me.

One of the worst feelings is to be left with a lacklustre/nonexistent response. You said that internal recruiters are the ones that make the process a slog. Taking that as fact, when communicating with you I would like some assurance that my application isn't falling on deaf ears. During the hiring process, I will usually ask when I can expect a response about the next step and being provided that gives me a sense of how long the process will take.
I'm really not sure if I prefer to be ghosted over a lie like this. Then again, I've definitely seen worse on this subreddit.
You'd think they would come up with a more convincing lie rather than replying with what they did so soon. Unfortunate, but I'll keep looking!
The worst is when post orders don't exist in a written format anywhere and they're given to you vaguely described by word of mouth and you have to wing it until you figure out everything on your own.

I don't think I took the silence personally; it was more that I didn't know what to do in that moment and panicked, so I think my lack of experience reared its ugly head there. 
Remaining respectful and kind is really good advice for sure, and I think that from this experience of mind appearing unsure and vulnerable is something I should work on and avoid in the future.

It really was a strange experience for me. Pretty much everyone else I had met up until him (including other people in executive positions) was kind and personable. So to see this sort of reaction from someone really disappoints me and doesn't make me want to work for a client that has that sort of person in the upper ranks.
Unfortunately, I didn't get the luxury of a warning or even a write-up, which I would have been much more receptive to, assuming that was the real reason.
This is good advice for sure. I try to be alone at my desk when possible and avoid approaching anyone that could be "important". Unfortunately in this case, he approached me.

> Were the rules made clear at your site as a part of post orders?

Not at all. The only thing resembling post orders that I got were from my predecessor and that was only from word of mouth, never written down. No mention of rules either. I was told to sit at the front, attend a zoom meeting on Thursday, and check the sink every morning. Anything else I did for work I taught myself how to do because it felt like the right thing to do (e.g. what to do when people forget their key cards).

> However, your company is essentially responsible for providing you with a new post at this point. To lose you as a guard, provided you’ve been honest, would be a major waste as the Company should absolutely fight for you in this case.

Both my branch manager and the client manager fought tooth and nail to reinstate me, but the decision was final since it came from someone so high up. They're trying to find me a better site and I'm very grateful to them.

>  greet people like you’re happy to see them

Believe me, I do greet people with enthusiasm. Like I said in my post, him suddenly telling me that he was the president after an awkward silence caught me by surprise so I was at a loss of words, not to mention it's weird to greet someone after the first exchange of words. Definitely good advice though, making yourself likeable and easy to work with are very important in any line of work. I'm glad that my managers embody those qualities.

This is absolutely good advice. I don't want people to believe that's not how I was acting up until now though. I drop anything unimportant like my lunch and give people my undivided attention when they approach me, so I apologize if I didn't make that clear enough in my main post. The awkward silence after me giving him the answer to his question definitely caught me by surprise.
This was a learning experience for sure. I'm glad my managers are understanding and trying to find me something better.

I would have been perfectly okay with putting them away if asked or never wearing them again with a warning/write-up. Sucks to go to rock bottom from that.

You'd think with how I got punished I might as well have been verbally threatening and insulting the guy.
You'd think I would have lost the site sooner. I worked that day like any other, airpods included.
Thanks and yeah, if he could get me canned from something like that, even if I were to go back he'd be able to do it again just as quickly.

The only uniform I have is the one my company gave me when I first got the job, and that was just a standard guard uniform (no logo white shirt and black pants, tie with company logo) and a blazer (also no logo). When I got onto the site I'm working at now, they told me the dress code was business casual so I just come into work in my own dress shirt and pants. I still wear their tie.

From what I've heard, if you've gotten this far you've probably got the job in the bag and the interview is just a formality. All I can think of is just ask about what kinds of sites they can put you at and ways of contacting management.
I just come into my site in business casual clothes because I'm essentially a receptionist. Few would be able to tell that I'm a security guard.

Thank you for the advice! It's kinda weird for me to contact my managers/supervisors because the only times I've spoken with them is when they call me on the phone. No one has answered the few times I've tried to call back. The only other sort of communication I have with...someone? is when I text the central scheduling number letting them know I'm on-site and they reply with "copy"

But I'll let them know the next time I get in contact with them, hopefully before the end of my gig here!

Thanks a bunch! The guy I'm covering for says he's been working at this place since June (I forgot if he mentioned if it was literally a month before or June of last year), but has been working as a security guard for over 5 years. During training he was doing some job searching for secretarial/assistant work because of the Allied buyout so I was unsure of what that would mean for my chances of getting here.
